Munition
mū-nĭsh'ən
n. (a fortification, a stronghold; in the Authorized Version the defence itself rather than the ammunition)
Latin munitio, a fortifying, from munire, to wall or defend. The English word later shifted to mean ammunition; in the Authorized Version it keeps the older sense of the wall a city keeps.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah uses it of Jerusalem under siege: “And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision” (Isa 29:7). The armies that seemed unanswerable will prove as substantial as a dream a man wakes from. Nahum uses it in a burst of four commands to a doomed city: “He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily” (Nah 2:1). Every order is sound military advice, and Nineveh is going to fall anyway; the prophet is speaking with the terrible irony of a God who tells a city to do its best. The word therefore stands in Scripture at exactly the place where human defence is at its most competent and least sufficient. Isaiah 33 supplies what is the true munition: the place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks, said of the man who walks righteously, whose bread and water are sure.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines munition as fortification, a place of defence, a stronghold; and secondarily, materials used in war, ammunition and military stores.

expand to see more

MUNITION, n. [L. munitio, from munio, to fortify.] Fortification; a place of defence; a stronghold.

Keep the munition, watch the way. Nah. ii.

2. Ammunition; whatever materials are used in war for defence, or for annoying an enemy.

MUNIMENT, n. A fortification of any kind; a stronghold; a place of defence.

Key Scripture

Isa 29:7 — "And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision."

Nah 2:1 — "He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily."

Psa 127:1 — "A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."

Zec 4:6 — "Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 127 is quoted to excuse doing nothing, though it names the builder, the watchman and their labour and denies only that the labour is what secures the result.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right relation between defence and dependence. Psalm 127 does not say that building and watching are useless; it says that except the LORD build and keep, they are in vain. The builder still builds. The watchman still wakes. Nahum tells Nineveh to keep the munition and watch the way, and every one of those imperatives is what a responsible city would do. What Scripture denies is that the wall is what saves. A Christian household, a congregation, a nation may take every prudent measure and must not then rest on the measures; and it may not use the doctrine of providence as a reason to leave the gate open.

Isaiah's image is the comfort. The nations that fight against Ariel and her munition shall be as a dream of a night vision — a hungry man dreaming that he eats, who wakes and is empty still. The armies were real enough to break a wall; before God they had no more substance than a dream. That is not a promise that every siege is lifted; Jerusalem did fall in Jeremiah's day, and the church has often been overrun. It is a statement about the final weight of things. The powers that press upon the people of God look solid and are not; and the defence that looks slight — the man who walks righteously, whose bread shall be given him and whose waters shall be sure — has his dwelling in the munitions of rocks. Nineveh kept her munition, watched her way, made her loins strong, and Nahum records the result three chapters long.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew metsurah (H4694) and matsor (H4692), a fortification, a siege-work; from tsur, to bind or besiege — the same root serving both the wall and the siege against it.

expand to see more

Hebrew metsurah (H4694) — a stronghold, a fortification; keep the munition; Nahum 2:1.

Hebrew matsod (H4685) — a siege work, a bulwark; all that fight against her and her munition; Isaiah 29:7.

Hebrew tsur (H6696) — to bind, to besiege; the root behind both the wall and the siege.

Hebrew misgab (H4869) — a high place, a defence; the LORD is a refuge and a high tower; Psalm 9:9.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to watch; except the LORD keep the city; Psalm 127:1.

Usage

"“All that fight against her and her munition… shall be as a dream of a night vision” — armies with the weight of a dream."

"“Keep the munition, watch the way” — sound orders to a city that fell."

"“Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” — and the watchman still wakes."
